subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
subtype: Approach: asking the police or shop counter to display a notice [Action]
passage: Come here and listen. When I was ten, I, your grandmother Shalini, was waiting at the bus stand with my mother's bundle when I saw a cloth bag under the bench. I peeked inside: bundles of notes. My knees turned to water. I did not touch it again. I ran to the chai seller, Ramu Kaka, and said, "Please phone the police post. Somebody must be missing this." Constable Hrithik came, wrote down what I said and took the bag, telling us that whoever came had to describe what was inside. Two days later a farmer came, weeping, and named every bundle. I never saw that money again, and I never missed it.

qa.q: Where did Shalini see the cloth bag?
qa.a: Shalini saw it under the bench at the bus stand.

qa.q: What did Shalini feel when the bundles of notes came into view?
qa.a: Shocked and scared, since Shalini's knees turned to water and Shalini did not touch the bag again.

qa.q: What choice at the bus stand made sure the money reached its owner?
qa.a: Shalini asked the chai seller to phone the police post, which held the bag until the right person could describe what was inside.

qa.q: How might the farmer have felt when the bag was returned?
qa.a: Relieved and overwhelmed, since the farmer came weeping and named every bundle.

grounding: A child finds a bag of cash and has the tea seller call the police post, which holds it for the owner to claim.

passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof of the Shivpur bus stand when Yogesh spotted a cloth bag wedged under the bench. Inside were bundles of notes held with rubber bands. His school bus was due in ten minutes. Yogesh looked around; nobody seemed to be searching. He closed the bag and carried it to the tea stall. "Bhaiya, someone lost this. Can you call the police?" The stall owner, Sachin, wiped his hands and dialled the chowki. Yogesh waited, one eye on the road, until a constable arrived on a scooter, counted the bundles in front of them both and wrote Yogesh's name in a register. "The owner will have to tell us the colour of the bag and what is inside," the constable said. Yogesh ran for his bus, soaked but light on his feet.

qa.q: What was inside the cloth bag?
qa.a: Bundles of notes held with rubber bands.

qa.q: What might Yogesh have been worried about while he waited at the stall?
qa.a: He was anxious about missing his school bus, yet he kept waiting because he wanted the money to reach safe hands first.

qa.q: What else could Yogesh have done if the tea stall had been closed?
qa.a: He could have taken the bag to the ticket counter or a bus conductor at the stand, since a known adult in a fixed place can pass it to the police.

qa.q: How does this plan look to the person who lost the bag?
qa.a: They can get it back only by describing the bag and what is inside, so nobody can simply walk up and claim it.

grounding: A child who finds cash at a bus stand gets a nearby stall owner to call the police, who keep it until the owner can describe it.

passage: Lunchtime at the Karol Nagar bus stop. Tenzin was waiting for his aunt when he noticed a zipped pouch lying beside the bench leg. He opened it just enough to see a thick fold of notes and a bus pass with no name. His heart thumped. Chetan-uncle, who ran the tea stall across the footpath, was pouring glasses for two drivers. Tenzin walked over and held out the pouch. "I found this. Will you ring the police chowki? I don't want to keep it." Chetan-uncle made the call, and a constable came and took the pouch away. Twenty minutes later, while Tenzin was still at the stop, a woman hurried back, searching under the bench. Tenzin pointed her to the stall. At the chowki she described the pouch and the pass, and got it back.

qa.q: Who ran the tea stall across the footpath?
What does Tenzin's thumping heart suggest?
qa.a: He felt nervous and uneasy holding so much money that was not his, which is why he did not want to keep it.

qa.q: Which approach would suit Tenzin if the stall had been empty?
qa.a: He could wait for his aunt and ask her to take the pouch to the chowki with him, because a child should hand found money to a trusted adult rather than carry it around.

qa.q: What is it like for the woman when she finds the bench empty?
qa.a: She is probably panicked at first, then relieved when Tenzin points her to the stall and she gets the pouch back by describing it.

grounding: The passage shows a child asking a tea-stall owner to phone the police so the rightful owner can later identify and claim the money.
